All flights are on 2026 dates, operated by Qantas (QF) and British Airways (BA). Reservation codes: Gary & Karen – KXFECY / EKNMYW; Deb & Tom – UWBGQP / EKH3PP (the Akhursts join the group in Sydney, so have no Wellington–Sydney sector). Frequent flyer numbers, seat assignments and check-in requirements are held in the original Sabre itinerary emails.

Sydney layover (Thu 10 Sept, ~7 hrs): Yes, you can leave the airport. As NZ passport holders, Gary & Karen are automatically granted a Special Category (subclass 444) visa on arrival, so there's no separate visa to arrange. A ~7 hour layover is comfortably above the ~5 hour minimum generally recommended to clear immigration, get into the city and back through security in time (allow ~45 min for immigration on arrival, ~60 min for security before the next departure).

Singapore transit on BA15 (Mon 28 Sept, ~1h 40m): Everyone must deplane at Changi with all carry-on items – there's no option to stay onboard. On one ticket with bags checked through you won't need to clear passport control, but you WILL need to re-clear security before boarding the onward Sydney sector, as security is at the gate in Singapore. Queues can be long since the whole aircraft transits at once – follow the crew's instruction on what time to be back at the gate.

Friday 11th September (Day 2)Rome
🎉 Fun Facts
Villa Borghese Gardens were laid out from 1605 by Cardinal Scipione Borghese – nephew of Pope Paul V – as one of the first great "gardens of delight" in Europe, built purely for pleasure, art and parties rather than growing food. — Wikipedia
The Galleria Borghese inside the gardens holds Bernini's Apollo and Daphne, carved when he was just 24, and a marble statue of Napoleon's sister Pauline Bonaparte reclining semi-nude that scandalised Rome when it was unveiled in 1808. — Galleria Borghese

💡 The odd name comes from a medieval legend: a bishop travelling to Rome sent his servant ahead to chalk "Est!" (Latin for "it is [good]") on the doors of inns with good wine. At Montefiascone the wine was so good the servant wrote "Est! Est!! Est!!!" three times - the bishop loved it so much he settled there for the rest of his life.

Saturday 12th September (Day 3)Rome
🎉 Fun Facts
It's a myth that Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling lying flat on his back. He actually designed a custom scaffold and painted standing up, craning his neck backwards for four years – the "lying down" idea came from a mistranslated 1527 biography. — History.com
St Peter's Basilica, next to the Sistine Chapel, took 120 years to build (1506-1626) and passed through the hands of 24 different architects, including Bramante, Raphael, Michelangelo and finally Bernini, who added the great colonnaded piazza. — Wikipedia
The Sistine Chapel ceiling you'll see this morning covers roughly 1,100 square metres and features over 300 individual figures - Michelangelo painted it almost entirely solo between 1508 and 1512, with only a handful of assistants mixing plaster and paint. — Vatican Museums

Sunday 13th September (Day 4)Rome
🎉 Fun Facts
The Colosseum had a retractable fabric awning called the velarium, made of the same sailcloth used on Roman warships. It weighed about 24 tonnes and was rigged and operated by a special detachment of around 1,000 sailors from the Roman navy. — Wikipedia
Beneath the Colosseum's arena floor lies the hypogeum – a two-level maze of tunnels and animal cages with as many as 80 vertical shafts and lift mechanisms that could hoist lions, bears and other beasts straight up into trapdoors in the arena. — Wikipedia

💳 Onboard Costs & Local Taxes

Your AU-market fare already includes port taxes and government fees – no port on this itinerary charges a landing tax at the gangway. Italian and French tourist taxes only apply if you sleep ashore, which you don't on any of these port days.

  • Onboard hotel/service charge: US$18 per person, per day – roughly US$252 for the two of you across the 7-night voyage, billed to your onboard account in USD.
  • Drinks: 18% gratuity added automatically to every bar/drinks charge on board.
  • Ashore: entry tickets, transport and any ATM/FX conversion costs are on you – including the new €2 Trevi Fountain entry ticket if you're revisiting Rome-area sights.
  • Booking conditions clause 36 lets Cunard pass on any tourist/landing taxes introduced after booking, and change the service charge rate before you sail.

Two things worth acting on: EES biometrics have been live at EU borders since April 2026, so allow extra time at Civitavecchia on embarkation day; and My Cunard onboard tour prices close about 4 days before sailing (~10 Sep) at roughly 10% below the on-board price, so book any extra shore tours before then.

📌 Booked Tours & Port Notes
  • Wed 16 Sep – Marseille: Little Train tour booked.
  • Thu 17 Sep – Villefranche/Monaco: Monaco Old Town tour booked. Villefranche is a tender port – the ship anchors offshore and you'll be ferried in by tender boat, so allow extra time to get ashore.
  • Fri 18 Sep – Genoa: Discover Genoa tour booked.
  • Sat 19 Sep – La Spezia: Easy Pisa tour booked, departs 7:45am.

Monday 14th September (Day 5)Rome
🎉 Fun Facts
Civitavecchia, where you'll board Queen Victoria, was built as a Roman port around 103-110 AD on the orders of Emperor Trajan, who commissioned the famous architect Apollodorus of Damascus to design it. It was originally called Centumcellae. — Roman Ports
Civitavecchia handles well over 2 million cruise passengers a year, making it one of the busiest cruise ports in the Mediterranean, despite the town itself having a population of only around 50,000. — Port of Civitavecchia
Queen Victoria, the ship you'll board today, carries just over 2,000 passengers - modest by modern cruise-ship standards, deliberately built smaller and more traditionally styled than Cunard's flagship Queen Mary 2. — Cunard

Wednesday 16th September (Day 7)Marseille, France
🎉 Fun Facts
Marseille, today's port of call, is the oldest city in France – founded around 600 BC by Greek settlers from Phocaea, who named it Massalia. That makes it roughly 2,600 years old. — Wikipedia
Marseille soap, savon de Marseille, has been made to essentially the same olive-oil recipe since a 1688 royal decree from Louis XIV fixed the exact ingredients allowed to carry the name. — Wikipedia
Marseille's Notre-Dame de la Garde basilica, perched on the city's highest point, is topped by a 9.5-metre gilded statue of the Madonna and Child that has watched over sailors leaving and returning to the port since 1870. — Wikipedia

Thursday 17th September (Day 8)Villefranche, France
🎉 Fun Facts
Monégasques – the actual citizens of Monaco – are legally banned from gambling in their own Monte Carlo Casino, a rule dating back to the mid-1800s. The casino was built specifically to draw money from wealthy foreign visitors instead. — Fact Republic
Monaco is the world's second-smallest country after Vatican City, at just over 2 square kilometres - and it has grown roughly 20% larger since 1861 through land reclaimed from the sea. — Wikipedia
The Monaco Grand Prix, first raced in 1929, runs on ordinary public streets barricaded off once a year - drivers reach speeds of over 290 km/h just metres from the harbour where cruise ships dock. — Wikipedia

Friday 18th September (Day 9)Genoa, Italy
🎉 Fun Facts
Genoa, today's port, is traditionally held to be the birthplace of Christopher Columbus around 1451 – Columbus himself wrote in his 1498 will "yo nacio en Genoba" ("I was born in Genoa"), though the claim is still debated by historians. — Christopher Columbus
Genoa's medieval old town, the caruggi, is one of the largest and best-preserved historic centres in Europe - a dense maze of narrow lanes that helped the city earn UNESCO World Heritage status in 2006. — UNESCO
Genoa's La Lanterna lighthouse, visible from the port today, was first built in 1128 and rebuilt to its current 76-metre form in 1543 - making it one of the oldest lighthouses still operating anywhere in the world. — Wikipedia

Saturday 19th September (Day 10)La Spezia (Florence or Pisa)
🎉 Fun Facts
The Leaning Tower of Pisa took almost 200 years to build (1173-1372) because construction was interrupted twice by war for decades at a time. Those pauses accidentally saved it – they gave the soft soil time to settle, which stopped the tower toppling before it was even finished. — Wikipedia
Before restoration work in the 1990s-2000s, the Leaning Tower of Pisa was tilting at nearly 5.5 degrees. Engineers carefully removed soil from beneath the raised side to reduce the lean to its current, more stable 3.97 degrees. — Wikipedia

Monday 21st September (Day 12)Tuscany
🎉 Fun Facts
Talamone, where you'll stop for lunch, gets a mocking mention in Dante's Purgatorio. The Sienese had just bought the port for 8,000 florins hoping to build their fortunes there, but it was plagued by silt and malaria and never really worked out. — Princeton Dante Project
Talamone's hilltop Rocca Aldobrandesca fortress, overlooking the harbour where you'll arrive, was refortified by the Sienese in the 1300s and later garrisoned by the Spanish in the 1500s as part of their coastal defences. — Wikipedia
Nearby San Gimignano once bristled with as many as 72 stone towers, built by rival medieval families competing to build the tallest as a show of wealth and power. Only 14 towers survive today, giving the town its famous 'medieval Manhattan' skyline. — Wikipedia

Tuesday 22nd September (Day 13)Tuscany
🎉 Fun Facts
The black rooster on every bottle of Chianti Classico comes from a medieval legend: Florence and Siena settled a border dispute by each sending a knight to ride out at the crow of a rooster. Florence starved theirs so it crowed early in the dark, giving their knight a head start – and Florence most of Chianti. — Visit Tuscany
Chianti Classico must legally be aged at least a year before release, and the black rooster 'Gallo Nero' seal is only allowed on wine from the original historic Chianti Classico zone - not the wider Chianti region that surrounds it. — Consorzio Vino Chianti Classico
The rows of cypress trees lining Tuscany's hillsides were originally planted as windbreaks and property boundary markers by landowners centuries ago, long before they became the region's postcard image. — Visit Tuscany

Wednesday 23rd September (Day 14)Milan
🎉 Fun Facts
In the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II next to the Duomo, tradition says spinning three times on your right heel on a certain mosaic bull's more sensitive anatomy brings good luck. It's so popular the mosaic has needed repeated restoration from all the grinding heels. — VisitMilano
Milan's Duomo took nearly 600 years to finish, from 1386 to 1965. Napoleon, crowned King of Italy inside it in 1805, ordered the facade rushed to completion and personally financed the work to have it ready in time. — Wikipedia

Alternative Options for 23 September

Four alternative full-day plans in place of the base Tuscany → Milan drive above – pick one.

Note on Option C: Venice is a significant detour east before doubling back west to Milan – approx. 610 km / ~6h 20m total driving (vs. ~1h 30m for the base plan, ~5h 15m for Option A, ~3h 40m for Option B). Also note Venice's historic centre is car-free, so the car must be left at Tronchetto or Piazzale Roma and the centre reached on foot/vaporetto. Worth confirming everyone's comfortable with the long day before booking.

OPTION A - LAKE COMO, LUNCH AT HARRY'S (23 SEP) [Total driving: 5h 15m]
🎉 Fun Facts
Lake Como's Laglio, just along the shore from Harry's Bar Cernobbio, is home to George Clooney's 18th-century Villa Oleandra, bought in 2002 for around $10 million and now estimated at over $100 million. He's become an honorary citizen of the town. — Wevillas
Lake Como is one of the deepest lakes in Europe, plunging to over 400 metres in places - deep enough that its lake bed actually sits below sea level. — Wikipedia

OPTION B - FERRARI MUSEUM, MARANELLO (23 SEP) [Total driving: 3h 40m]
🎉 Fun Facts
Ferrari's prancing horse logo wasn't Enzo Ferrari's idea originally. It came from WWI flying ace Francesco Baracca, who painted a horse on his fighter plane. After he was killed in 1918, his mother suggested the young racer Enzo Ferrari use it for luck – he kept the horse but changed its colour to black, in Baracca's memory. — Rosso Automobili
Every Ferrari road car is still largely hand-assembled at the Maranello factory, where fewer than 15 cars typically roll off the line each day - production is deliberately kept scarce. — Ferrari

OPTION C - VENICE LUNCH (23 SEP) [Total driving: 6h 20m]
🎉 Fun Facts
Venice has no cars at all in its historic centre – it's built across 118 small islands linked by more than 400 bridges, and the only way around is on foot or by boat. That's exactly why you'll need to park at Tronchetto or Piazzale Roma before walking in. — Wikipedia
Venice is slowly sinking at roughly 1-2mm a year while the Adriatic rises around it, which is why the city completed the MOSE flood barrier system in 2020 to hold back high tides during 'acqua alta'. — Wikipedia

Getting Around: Tube Map & Travel Pass
Nearest station to the hotel: Great Portland Street (Circle, Hammersmith & City, Metropolitan lines) – approx. 2-3 min walk (~0.2 km), directly opposite The Level at Meliá White House.
🗺️ CLICK HERE for the Official TfL Tube Map (PDF)
Getting a travel pass for the few days:

Contactless bank card / Apple Pay / Google Pay – simplest option for most visitors. Just tap in and out at the yellow readers on the Tube, buses, DLR, Overground and Elizabeth line – no need to buy anything in advance. Fares are automatically capped at around £8.90/day for Zones 1-2 (2026 rate), so a few days of sightseeing between Zone 1 (central London) and Zone 2 (Regent's Park/Camden area) should never cost more than the daily cap, even if you tap in and out a lot. Check your bank doesn't charge foreign transaction fees before relying on this.

Visitor Oyster card – order online before you fly (from about £5 plus however much credit you preload) or buy a standard Oyster card at any station on arrival (£7 refundable deposit). Works exactly like contactless with the same daily cap, and avoids any card fees or acceptance issues. Top up at station machines or the TfL Oyster app.

7 Day Travelcard – only worth considering if doing lots of travel every single day; for a 4-day stay like this one, pay-as-you-go (contactless or Oyster) with the daily cap works out cheaper and more flexible.

Thursday 24th September (Day 15)London
🎉 Fun Facts
Tonight's dinner spot, The Lighterman, is named after the Victorian "lightermen" who steered flat-bottomed barges (called lighters) along the Regent's Canal right outside, ferrying goods through this once-industrial part of King's Cross. — King's Cross
Regent's Canal, which runs right past tonight's dinner spot, was built in the 1810s-1820s and named for the Prince Regent (later George IV). It once floated coal and building materials into London before being revived as a leisure towpath. — Wikipedia

Friday 25th September (Day 16)London
🎉 Fun Facts
The Mousetrap, playing tonight, is the world's longest continuously-running play – it opened in 1952 and passed 30,000 performances in 2025. By long tradition, the audience is asked at the end of every single show never to reveal the killer's identity. — Wikipedia
The V&A Museum was founded in 1852 using profits from the Great Exhibition of 1851, and its collection has since grown to more than 2.8 million objects spanning 5,000 years of art and design. — V&A
The V&A's Cast Courts hold a full plaster cast of Rome's Trajan's Column, taken in the 1860s - it's so tall it had to be split into two pieces just to fit under the gallery ceiling. — V&A

Saturday 26th September (Day 17)London
🎉 Fun Facts
The original Hard Rock Cafe in London opened on June 14, 1971, inside a deserted Rolls-Royce dealership. The founders only received a 6-month lease because their landlord did not think an American-style burger joint would last.
The ravens at the Tower of London have had their wings trimmed since at least the 1600s, following the legend that the kingdom will fall if they ever leave. Traditionally at least six are kept there, plus one in reserve. — Historic Royal Palaces
Six, the West End musical you're seeing tonight, reimagines the six wives of Henry VIII as a girl-group pop concert. It began life as a student production at Cambridge University in 2017 before transferring to the West End in 2019. — Wikipedia

Sunday 27th September (Day 18)Air Travel – Depart LHR (T5) 10.00pm
🎉 Fun Facts
When Heathrow first opened to passengers in 1946, the "terminal" was literally a row of ex-military tents along the Bath Road, furnished with floral armchairs, small tables of fresh flowers and even a branch of WH Smith – 63,000 passengers passed through in its first year. — Business Traveller
The Castle pub in Farringdon (today's Option 1 lunch) is the only pub in London licensed as a pawnbroker - supposedly granted personally by King George IV after he pawned his watch there to settle a gambling debt. — Wikipedia
Heathrow, where you'll fly out from tonight, handles more international passengers than any other airport on Earth - despite operating from just two runways, making it one of the busiest dual-runway airports in the world. — Heathrow Airport

Option 1: Lunch at The Castle or The Sir John Oldcastle, Farringdon
Two pub options right by Farringdon station – a laid-back lunch stop before heading to the airport.
Getting there: Great Portland Street → Farringdon on the Metropolitan/Circle/Hammersmith & City line, direct (no change), ~6 min journey, then ~2-3 min walk from Farringdon station to either pub.
The Castle ///range.return.colleague
Grade II listed pub & restaurant, est. 1865 – British pub food, craft beer, full bar, only pawnbroker's licence in London
34-35 Cowcross St, Farringdon, London EC1M 6DB
🕑 Sun 12pm-10:30pm (check ahead for any Sept 2026 changes)
📞 +44 20 7553 7621

The Sir John Oldcastle ///twin.milk.hurry
JD Wetherspoon pub, named after the historical figure said to have inspired Shakespeare's Falstaff – British pub food, full bar, right next to Farringdon station
29-35 Farringdon Rd, Farringdon, London EC1M 3JF

Cars Baby Cars

Supercar and luxury-marque showrooms clustered around Berkeley Square, Mayfair – all within roughly a 15-minute walk of Piccadilly Circus.

Rolls-Royce Motor Cars London
Flagship Rolls-Royce showroom on the corner of Berkeley Street and Stratton Street (~10 min walk)
50 Berkeley St, London W1J 8HD
WebsiteMap
Jack Barclay Bentley
London's oldest Bentley dealership (since 1927), on Berkeley Square (~10 min walk)
18 Berkeley Square, London W1J 6AE
WebsiteMap

Official Ferrari flagship showroom, Berkeley Square (~10 min walk)
15-17 Berkeley Square, London W1J 6EG
WebsiteMap
Lamborghini Mayfair
H.R. Owen flagship Lamborghini showroom, Berkeley Square (~10 min walk)
20 Berkeley Square, London W1J 6BR
WebsiteMap
Volvo Cars Central London
Official Volvo showroom and service centre, Swiss Cottage (a drive/tube ride, not walkable)

Rolls-Royce, Bentley, Ferrari and Lamborghini are all genuinely walkable from Piccadilly Circus around Berkeley Square, Mayfair. Volvo and Mercedes-Benz are London dealerships but sit further out (Swiss Cottage and Wandsworth) - worth a taxi/tube rather than a walk. Zeekr doesn't have a UK showroom yet - its London launch is expected later in 2026.

ZTL / Limited Traffic Zones (Italy)

You asked about "LTZ" areas – in Italy these are officially called ZTL (Zona a Traffico Limitato), or Limited Traffic Zones. Every historic Italian city centre has one, and they're the single easiest way to rack up fines while self-driving.

A ZTL is a camera-enforced zone – usually the old walled/historic centre – where only residents, permit holders and registered vehicles may drive during posted hours. Drive through the wrong gate and a camera reads the plate; the fine (typically €80–335, sometimes one per gate crossed) goes to the hire company, who forwards it to us plus their own admin fee – and it can turn up months after we're home. Watch for the sign: a white circle with a red border reading "Zona Traffico Limitato".

Schematic map – approximate positions, not to scale
Rome (Centro Storico)
🕑 Italy's most famous ZTL – not on our drive route
Daytime hours Mon–Fri, with extended evening ZTL in some nightlife sectors on weekends – camera-enforced across the historic centre.
🚗 We don't collect the hire car until Civitavecchia, so this one's FYI only – but it's the zone every guide warns about first, and worth knowing about generally.
Milan – Area C
🕑 Congestion charge + ZTL ring around the Duomo
Mon–Fri 7:30am–7:30pm, about €7.50/entry (higher on weekends), camera-enforced seven days a week from 2026.
🚗 The iQ Hotel Milano (Via Pirelli) sits just outside the Area C ring, so arriving/leaving the hotel should be fine – it only becomes a problem if we drive in towards the Duomo.
Como & Cernobbio (Option A)
🕑 Como old town ZTL – enforced daily, 9am–10pm
Covers the walled Città Murata, Piazza Duomo and Via Vittorio Emanuele II. The Cernobbio/Tremezzo lakeside road (SS340) itself is open, but narrow and often busy.
🚗 Best to park in a signed lot outside the old town (e.g. Autosilo Valduce) rather than drive in for Harry's Bar/the lakefront.
Bologna (Option B breakfast stop)
🕑 ZTL Centro Storico – every day, 7am–8pm
Camera-enforced ("Sirio" system) across the historic centre; a few streets are pedestrian-only around the clock.
🚗 Our Option B breakfast stop, Aroma Specialty Coffee on Via Portanova, sits inside this zone – better to park just outside and walk the last few minutes than drive to the door.
Modena & Maranello (Option B)
🕑 Modena's old town ZTL is effectively permit-holders-only
Modena's historic centre is restricted for most of the day; Maranello itself has no formal ZTL, but very heavy paid parking near the Ferrari Museum.
🚗 Best to follow the signed ring road/tangenziale around Modena rather than cut through its centre on the way to Maranello.
Florence
🕑 ZTL – 5 sectors, Mon–Fri 7:30am–8pm, Sat 7:30am–4pm
Free to drive Sundays and public holidays. Covers Piazza del Duomo, Piazza della Signoria and most of the historic core.
🚗 Not on our base route, but easy to stumble into if we detour into central Florence for a look.
Siena
🕑 Historic centre is effectively car-free
The whole medieval core sits inside a strict ZTL – park in one of the signed "parcheggio scambiatore" lots outside the walls and walk in.
🚗 Relevant if we make the short detour south from our hotel to see the Palio square (Piazza del Campo).
San Gimignano
🕑 No visitor cars inside the walls, ever (Apr–Oct)
Five paid car parks (P1–P5) sit just outside the medieval gates – it's a walk up from there, whichever one we use.
🚗 The 'medieval Manhattan' towers from our Day 12 Fun Facts – a natural detour from our Tuscany hotel, so worth knowing before we drive up.
Venice (Option C)
🕑 No cars at all in the historic centre – more a total ban than a ZTL
The car has to be left on the mainland at Tronchetto or Piazzale Roma car parks; the centre itself is reached on foot or by vaporetto (water bus).
🚗 Already flagged on our Option C route notes – the most extreme version of a 'limited traffic zone' in Italy.

General rule of thumb: park in a signed paid car park outside the old walls/centre and walk in, rather than following the satnav to the door – it's almost always faster than dealing with a fine later.

Daily Quiz

A 5-question multi-choice quiz for every day of the trip, themed to wherever we are that day – Rome history, cruise trivia, French Riviera, Tuscany, London and more. Browse the questions below any time, or print two separate documents: one with just the questions, one with the answer key.

Answer Key

Hidden from normal browsing so the quiz stays a surprise – use Print Answers to check your scores.

Day 2 · Fri 11 Sep · Rome Arrival

  1. B – The Tiber. The Tiber (Tevere) flows right past our hotel on its way out to the sea at Ostia.
  2. C – Seven. The "Seven Hills of Rome" - Palatine, Capitoline, Aventine, Caelian, Esquiline, Viminal and Quirinal.
  3. C – Vatican City. Vatican City - the world's smallest country, and where we're headed tomorrow.
  4. B – The Colosseum. The Colosseum - on the itinerary for Day 4 (Sunday).
  5. B – Romulus and Remus. Romulus and Remus - Romulus supposedly founded the city in 753 BC and became its first king.

Day 3 · Sat 12 Sep · Vatican & Sistine Chapel

  1. C – Michelangelo. Michelangelo - he reportedly complained the whole time that he was a sculptor, not a painter.
  2. B – About 4 years. About 4 years, 1508-1512, mostly lying on his back on scaffolding.
  3. C – The Last Judgment. The Last Judgment, painted 1536-1541 - nearly 30 years after the ceiling.
  4. B – Vatican City. Vatican City - about 0.44 sq km, smaller than most golf courses.
  5. C – St Peter's Square. St Peter's Square - the colonnade's four rows of columns are designed to line up as a single row from two marked spots in the piazza.

Day 4 · Sun 13 Sep · Colosseum

  1. A – 80 AD. 80 AD, under Emperor Titus - construction had started under his father Vespasian about 8 years earlier.
  2. C – 50,000-80,000. Around 50,000-80,000 - similar to a large modern stadium.
  3. B – The Hypogeum. The Hypogeum - a two-level maze of passages used to hoist animals and scenery up through trapdoors.
  4. C – Vespasian. Vespasian, funded partly by treasure from the sack of Jerusalem.
  5. B – Travertine limestone. Travertine limestone, quarried near Tivoli and hauled to Rome along a purpose-built road.

Day 5 · Mon 14 Sep · Rome to the Cruise

  1. C – Queen Victoria. Queen Victoria - Cunard voyage V618D, our home for the next week.
  2. A – Cunard. Cunard - famous for transatlantic ocean liners since the 1840s.
  3. B – Lusitania. RMS Lusitania - torpedoed off Ireland; nearly 1,200 died, including 128 Americans.
  4. B – 1840. 1840, by Samuel Cunard - making it one of the oldest shipping brands still operating.
  5. C – Civitavecchia. Civitavecchia - Rome's cruise port, about an hour from the city.

Day 6 · Tue 15 Sep · Sea Day

  1. B – Strait of Gibraltar. The Strait of Gibraltar - only about 13km wide at its narrowest.
  2. C – Sicily. Sicily - just ahead of Sardinia in size.
  3. C – About 5,200m. About 5,200m, southwest of Greece.
  4. B – The Black Sea. The Black Sea, via Istanbul's two famous straits.
  5. B – Knots. Knots (nautical miles per hour) - one knot is about 1.85 km/h.

Day 7 · Wed 16 Sep · Marseille, France

  1. B – Second-largest. Second-largest, after Paris.
  2. C – Greeks (Phocaeans). Greek settlers from Phocaea - making it one of the oldest cities in France.
  3. B – La Marseillaise. La Marseillaise - now sung at every French sporting event and state occasion.
  4. B – Bouillabaisse. Bouillabaisse - originally a fisherman's stew made from the day's unsellable catch.
  5. A – Notre-Dame de la Garde. Notre-Dame de la Garde - locals call it 'la bonne mère' (the good mother).

Day 8 · Thu 17 Sep · Villefranche & Monaco

  1. B – Vatican City. Vatican City - Monaco is second, at about 2.1 sq km.
  2. B – The Grimaldis. The Grimaldis - one of the longest-reigning royal families in the world.
  3. B – Monaco Grand Prix. The Monaco Grand Prix - one of Formula 1's oldest and most prestigious races.
  4. B – Grace Kelly. Grace Kelly - she gave up her acting career to become Princess Grace.
  5. B – Income tax. No personal income tax for residents - part of why it's such an expensive place to live.

Day 9 · Fri 18 Sep · Genoa, Italy

  1. C – Christopher Columbus. Christopher Columbus - born in Genoa around 1451.
  2. B – Liguria. Liguria - the crescent-shaped region along the Italian Riviera.
  3. B – Pesto. Pesto (alla genovese) - traditionally made with basil, pine nuts, garlic, parmesan and olive oil.
  4. B – Medieval old towns. Its centro storico is regularly cited as one of the largest and best-preserved medieval old towns in Europe.
  5. B – Venice. Venice - the two republics fought several wars for control of Mediterranean trade.

Day 10 · Sat 19 Sep · La Spezia & Pisa

  1. B – Soft, unstable ground. Soft, waterlogged subsoil couldn't support the foundation evenly.
  2. C – 8. 8 storeys, including the belfry at the top.
  3. B – A cathedral bell tower (campanile). It's the freestanding campanile (bell tower) of Pisa Cathedral.
  4. B – Galileo Galilei. Galileo Galilei - the story is likely apocryphal, but he did live and study in Pisa.
  5. B – Cinque Terre. Cinque Terre - literally 'Five Lands': Monterosso, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and Riomaggiore.

Day 11 · Sun 20 Sep · Sea Day

  1. B – Nile. The Nile, by most classic measurements - though some newer surveys argue for the Amazon.
  2. D – Pacific. The Pacific - bigger than all the landmasses on Earth combined.
  3. C – France. France - thanks to its overseas territories scattered around the globe (12 in total).
  4. B – Australia/Oceania. Australia/Oceania.
  5. B – The Urals. The Ural Mountains, running through Russia.

Day 12 · Mon 21 Sep · Tuscany (Talamone & Chianti)

  1. C – Black. Black - the "Gallo Nero" seal, only allowed on wine from the original historic Chianti Classico zone.
  2. B – Sangiovese. Sangiovese - Italy's most widely planted red grape.
  3. B – Purgatorio. Purgatorio - the Sienese had just bought Talamone hoping to build their fortunes there; it never worked out.
  4. C – Florence. Florence.
  5. B – Agriturismo. Agriturismo - a working farm offering accommodation and food, like our lunch stop today.

Day 13 · Tue 22 Sep · Tuscany Free Day

  1. B – Towers. Its 'medieval Manhattan' skyline - rival families once competed to build the tallest tower.
  2. B – About 14. About 14 - most were later torn down or collapsed.
  3. B – Leonardo da Vinci. Leonardo da Vinci - born in the town of Vinci, in the province of Florence.
  4. A – Florence and Siena. Florence and Siena.
  5. B – The Medici. The Medici family - bankers, popes and patrons of Michelangelo, Botticelli and Galileo.

Day 14 · Wed 23 Sep · Milan (Options Day)

  1. C – Nearly 6 centuries. Started in 1386, with its final bronze door only added in 1965 - almost 600 years.
  2. B – Santa Maria delle Grazie. The refectory of the Santa Maria delle Grazie convent.
  3. B – Fashion. Fashion - home to Milan Fashion Week and many major Italian fashion houses.
  4. B – La Scala. La Scala, opened in 1778.
  5. B – George Clooney's. George Clooney's Villa Oleandra in Laglio - he's an honorary citizen of the town.

Day 15 · Thu 24 Sep · London Arrival

  1. B – The Thames. The Thames - our hotel and The Lighterman both sit right on it near Regent's Park/Kings Cross.
  2. C – 215 miles. About 215 miles (346 km) from its source in Gloucestershire to the North Sea.
  3. A – Big Ben. Big Ben is technically the bell - the tower itself is the Elizabeth Tower - but everyone calls the whole thing Big Ben.
  4. B – Piccadilly line. The Piccadilly line - dark blue, running past Piccadilly Circus.
  5. B – Buses. Buses - the modern Routemaster is a direct descendant of the original AEC Routemaster.

Day 16 · Fri 25 Sep · London (The Mousetrap)

  1. B – Play. It's a play, not a musical - the longest continuously-running show of any kind in the world.
  2. A – Agatha Christie. Agatha Christie - the undisputed 'Queen of Crime'.
  3. B – West End. The West End - London's answer to Broadway.
  4. B – 1950s. 1952 - and it has run continuously ever since (apart from a brief COVID closure).
  5. B – Keep the ending a secret. Keep the twist ending a secret - a tradition observed by audiences for over 70 years.

Day 17 · Sat 26 Sep · London (Tower Bridge & Six)

  1. C – Six. Six - "divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived", as the old rhyme goes.
  2. B – Anne Boleyn. Anne Boleyn - executed in 1536; Catherine Howard (wife five) was also later beheaded.
  3. B – London Bridge. London Bridge - a US buyer once reportedly thought he'd bought Tower Bridge when he actually bought London Bridge.
  4. B – The Tower of London. The Tower of London - nearly 1,000 years old.
  5. A – The Crown Jewels. The Crown Jewels - including the Imperial State Crown, worn at coronations.

Fun Facts by Day

Extra fun facts for the places we're seeing each day – on top of the ones shown in each day's Fun Facts box on screen.

Friday 11th September (Day 2)

Tucked inside Villa Borghese is a curious 1867 water clock, invented by the monk-scientist Giovan Battista Embriaco, which still keeps time today using only the flow and pressure of water – no electricity or batteries. — Turismo Roma
Cardinal Scipione Borghese amassed a private collection of over 800 sculptures and paintings by artists including Caravaggio, Bernini and Titian, which only became the public Galleria Borghese museum after the Italian state bought the estate from the family in 1902. — Wikipedia
Villa Borghese has a hydraulic 'water clock' (the Pincio Clepsydra) built in 1867-73 that has run continuously ever since, powered only by two seesawing basins of flowing water – it never needs winding. — Through Eternity Tours
Cardinal Scipione Borghese was such a ruthless art collector that he once had the painter Domenichino thrown in prison until he handed over a painting the cardinal wanted for his gallery. — RomeHints
Caravaggio's Madonna and Child with St Anne was rejected by St Peter's Basilica because church officials thought the Madonna looked too much like a real woman off the street – Cardinal Scipione Borghese snapped it up for his own collection instead. — Sightseeing Experience Magazine
The building now known as Casa del Cinema inside the gardens was once a dairy serving cream and custard, before it became a glitzy 1930s restaurant and later a Dolce Vita-era dance club called 'La Lucciola'. — Turismo Roma

Saturday 12th September (Day 3)

A ten-year restoration of the Sistine Chapel ceiling, completed in 1990 and sponsored by Japan's Nippon Television, stripped away centuries of soot, glue and candle grease to reveal Michelangelo's original vivid colours hidden underneath. — Wikipedia
Michelangelo became chief architect of St Peter's Basilica in 1547 at the age of 71, but only lived to see the drum of its dome completed; his design was finished by Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana in 1590, 26 years after his death. — Wikipedia
Michelangelo hated painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling so much he wrote a grumbling poem about it, complaining his stomach was 'squashed under his chin' and that he'd grown a goiter from the strain of looking up for months. — Dutch Fine Paintings
A later painter named Daniele da Volterra was hired to paint loincloths and drapery over the nude figures in Michelangelo's Last Judgment – earning him the permanent nickname 'Il Braghettone', or 'The Breeches-Maker'. — Wikipedia
In 1972 a man attacked Michelangelo's Pietà in St Peter's Basilica with a hammer, shouting he was Jesus Christ; the statue was restored and now sits behind bulletproof glass. — EWTN Vatican
The gold letters running around the base of St Peter's dome look like modest, ordinary lettering from the floor – each one is actually about 7 feet tall, roughly the height of an adult man. — EWTN Vatican

Sunday 13th September (Day 4)

The Colosseum's opening games in 80 AD reportedly included a naumachia, a staged naval battle, with the arena flooded for small ships – once the underground hypogeum was built under Emperor Domitian, further flooding became impossible and the practice stopped. — Wikipedia
The amphitheatre wasn't officially called the Colosseum in ancient times – it was the Flavian Amphitheatre – and the popular name actually comes from the Colossus of Nero, a giant bronze statue over 30 metres tall that once stood beside it. — Wikipedia
Beneath the Colosseum's arena floor was the hypogeum, a maze of tunnels and cages with pulley-operated lifts – gladiators and wild animals could pop up through trapdoors, seemingly out of nowhere, right in front of the crowd. — Through Eternity Tours
Before the underground hypogeum existed, the Colosseum could be flooded for mock naval battles called naumachiae, with small warships fighting it out in a man-made lake inside the arena. — National Geographic
In one bizarre event, the arena floor was landscaped like a forest and stocked with deer, boar and ostriches – spectators were handed tickets and let loose to hunt the animals themselves and take the meat home. — All That's Interesting
The Colosseum we see today is a bare stone skeleton, but in Roman times it was covered in polished marble and bronze details, making it gleam rather than look like a ruin. — The Colosseum

Monday 14th September (Day 5)

Civitavecchia's harbour fortress, Forte Michelangelo, was designed by the architect Bramante in 1508 and completed in 1537 under the supervision of Michelangelo himself, and it still stands guard over the port today. — Port of Rome - Civitavecchia
In 1696, Pope Innocent XII declared Civitavecchia a free port, exempting trading ships from certain taxes – a status that helped it grow into Rome's principal seaport. — Britannica
The French novelist Stendhal – famous for giving his name to 'Stendhal syndrome', the fainting fits caused by overwhelming art – once served as the French consul in Civitavecchia. — Roma Experience
Civitavecchia's harbour fortress is popularly called 'Fort Michelangelo', but that was never its official name – it was christened Fortress Giulia after Pope Julius II, who commissioned it; Michelangelo is only credited with the top tower. — Cabinet
In 1972, workers in Civitavecchia found frescoes hidden under layers of lime and wallpaper that turned out to be near-exact copies of Raphael's frescoes from the Vatican's Room of Heliodorus – nobody has ever figured out why they're there. — Port Mobility Civitavecchia
When Queen Victoria was officially named by the Duchess of Cornwall in 2007, the champagne bottle swung at the bow refused to smash – considered a maritime bad omen – so a backup bottle had to be released to finish the job. — UPI

Tuesday 15th September (Day 6)

Queen Victoria was christened in Southampton on 10 December 2007 by Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall, and set sail on her maiden voyage to the Canary Islands the very next day. — Wikipedia
The custom of afternoon tea dates back to the 1840s, credited to Anna, 7th Duchess of Bedford, who began taking tea and a light snack in her rooms to bridge the gap between lunch and dinner – a habit Queen Victoria herself later helped make fashionable. — British Museum
The roaring lion on the Golden Lion pub's signage traces back to the artwork on the launch programme for the original Queen Elizabeth in 1938 – Cunard's mascot has been guarding the ship's pub ever since. — Paul's Beer & Travel Blog
The Golden Lion pubs on Cunard ships serve beers brewed exclusively for the line, including an odd one called 'Breakfast' – a biscotti-flavoured stout. — Paul's Beer & Travel Blog
Tucked among Cunard's white-tie ballrooms and formal dining rooms is a proper English pub complete with a dartboard, karaoke nights and pub quizzes – a deliberately unpretentious contrast to the rest of the ship. — Cunard

Wednesday 16th September (Day 7)

Marseille's signature bouillabaisse traces back to a simple fisherman's stew the ancient Greeks called kakavia; in 1980 the city's restaurateurs even drew up an official Bouillabaisse Charter defining the authentic recipe and ingredients. — National Geographic
Marseille's Vieux Port was once spanned by a pioneering transporter bridge, inaugurated in 1905, which carried passengers and vehicles across the harbour entrance on a suspended gondola until German forces destroyed it in 1944. — Wikipedia
There's a Marseille saying that 'it was the sardine that blocked the port' – a real 1780 incident where a warship called the Sartine ran aground at the harbour mouth got garbled over time into a legend about a giant fish plugging the port. — Connexion France
Coffee first entered France through Marseille in 1644, and the city opened its first coffeehouse in 1671 – a full year before Paris got one. — All About Coffee

Thursday 17th September (Day 8)

In 1297, the Grimaldi family seized Monaco's fortress when François Grimaldi disguised himself as a Franciscan monk to sneak armed men inside – the origin of the sword-wielding monk still shown on Monaco's coat of arms today. — Wikipedia
Prince Rainier III's 1956 marriage to Hollywood actress Grace Kelly at Monaco's Saint Nicholas Cathedral was watched by more than 30 million television viewers worldwide, dubbed the 'wedding of the century'. — History.com
Monaco has no airport, so getting there means arriving by helicopter, superyacht or train – yet the tiny 2-square-kilometre country still packs in a network of public tunnels, escalators and lifts to move people up and down its cliffside terrain. — Trafalgar
Monaco's royal couple are both genuine Olympians – Prince Albert II competed in bobsleigh at five consecutive Winter Olympics, while Princess Charlene won swimming medals for South Africa before becoming a princess. — Trafalgar
Monaco is watched over by more than 560 CCTV cameras and has roughly one police officer for every 60 residents, giving it one of the highest security-personnel densities of any country on Earth. — Trafalgar

Friday 18th September (Day 9)

The word "jeans" traces back to Genoa itself: French traders called the sturdy cotton fabric woven there for sailors' trousers "bleu de Gênes" (blue of Genoa), later shortened to "jean". — Merriam-Webster
From the 11th century until Napoleon dissolved it in 1797, Genoa was the seat of its own maritime superpower, the Republic of Genoa, whose fleets and banks once rivalled Venice's. — Wikipedia
Genoa's medieval cathedral, San Lorenzo, still has an unexploded WWII naval shell embedded in its side wall – it crashed through during a 1941 bombardment and simply never went off. — Atlas Obscura
Beneath Genoa's streets lies a hidden network of WWII-era escape tunnels and bomb shelters, including a 150-metre passage burrowed under the Doge's Palace. — myCityHunt
Genoa's harbour lighthouse, La Lanterna, can claim the title of the tallest traditional lighthouse in the world, depending on how you measure it. — Atlas Obscura
Palazzo San Giorgio, once home to one of the oldest banks in the world, is also where Marco Polo is said to have dictated his famous travel memoirs. — Atlas Obscura

Saturday 19th September (Day 10)

The tower was already sinking before it even looked crooked: by the time builders reached the second floor in 1178, the soft subsoil beneath its shallow 3-metre foundation had begun to give way, decades before the famous lean became obvious. — Wikipedia
Legend says Galileo Galilei, who lived in Pisa, dropped two cannonballs of different masses from the tower around 1589-92 to prove they fall at the same speed – but the only source is a biography written by his student decades later, and historians still dispute whether it happened. — Wikipedia
The Leaning Tower of Pisa's largest bell weighs around 3,600kg – about the same as a full-grown female African elephant. — The Fact Site
In 1944, a 23-year-old American sergeant was ordered to check the tower for German snipers before possibly calling in an artillery strike – he couldn't bring himself to destroy something so beautiful, and the tower survived the war. — The Fact Site
Pisa's famous tilt isn't unique – the bell tower of the nearby Church of St Nicola leans too, thanks to the same soft ground. — Fact City
The tower's bells haven't rung properly in over 100 years – partly because one of them, the 'Bell of the Traitor', traditionally tolled whenever a criminal was executed. — Fact City

Sunday 20th September (Day 11)

Queen Victoria was the first Cunard ship to feature West End-style private theatre boxes, in her three-storey Royal Court Theatre – an innovation later copied on sister ship Queen Elizabeth. — Cunard
Each year, guests and crew aboard Queen Victoria get through around 1.5 million fresh eggs and close to a million cups of tea. — Cunard
Queen Victoria has the first two-storey library ever built at sea, stocked with around 6,000 books, journals and periodicals. — Chris Frame's Cunard Page
The ship's Winter Garden has a retractable glass roof that can be opened to the sky – a colonial-style conservatory built right into a working ocean liner. — Chris Frame's Cunard Page
Queen Victoria's six main suites are each named after a historic Cunard liner – Mauretania, Laconia, Aquitania, Berengaria, Carpathia and Caronia. — Chris Frame's Cunard Page

Monday 21st September (Day 12)

Talamone's Etruscan temple, built in the 4th century BC to honour the god Tinia, once bore a dramatic terracotta pediment depicting the myth of the "Seven Against Thebes"; the surviving reliefs are now housed in Florence's Archaeological Museum. — In Vacanza all'Argentario
San Gimignano grew rich on saffron: medieval merchants exported its "red gold" as far as Alexandria and Damietta, and the profits helped fund the stone tower-houses that still define the skyline. — Visit Tuscany
The 1280 Torre Chigi in San Gimignano has its front door on the first floor – residents climbed a ladder to get in and pulled it up at night so rival families couldn't attack them in their sleep. — Torciano Magazine
Talamone doubled as a Tuscan hideaway in the James Bond film Quantum of Solace – 007 arrives by boat near the medieval Torre di Talamonaccio on the coast. — James Bond Lifestyle
Admiral Horatio Nelson dropped anchor off Talamone in June 1798 while hunting for Napoleon's fleet, just weeks before his decisive victory at the Battle of the Nile. — My Kind of Italy

Tuesday 22nd September (Day 13)

The name "Chianti" first appears in writing as early as 1398, in a notarial document referring to wine from the area – centuries before the modern Chianti Classico appellation existed. — Consorzio Vino Chianti Classico
In 1716, Grand Duke Cosimo III de' Medici issued a decree formally defining the boundaries of the Chianti wine-producing zone, making it one of the earliest legally delimited wine regions in the world. — Consorzio Vino Chianti Classico
Renaissance master Giorgio Vasari painted the black rooster into his 1565 'Allegory of Chianti' ceiling panel in Florence's Palazzo Vecchio, cementing it as the region's symbol centuries before it appeared on a wine label. — Chianti Classico Consorzio
The Chianti Classico black rooster trademark is so tightly policed that, since 2005, a bottle without the rooster on its label legally isn't allowed to call itself Chianti Classico at all. — Chianti Classico Consorzio

Wednesday 23rd September (Day 14)

The golden Madonnina statue atop Milan's Duomo secretly doubles as a giant lightning rod – the metal halberd she holds was engineered to protect the cathedral from lightning strikes. — Duomo di Milano
From 1939, Milan's golden Madonnina was covered in grey-green camouflage cloth for five years during the Second World War, so Allied bombers couldn't use her golden glint to pinpoint the city. — Duomo di Milano
The Galleria's floor mosaics depict four cities of the newly unified Kingdom of Italy as animals – Turin as a bull, Rome as a wolf, Florence as a lily, and Milan as its own red cross. — The Art Post Blog

Wednesday 23rd September (Day 14) – Option A – Lake Como & Harry's Bar

The Roman writer Pliny the Younger owned two villas on Lake Como which he nicknamed "Comedy" and "Tragedy" – one perched high with sweeping views, the other so close to the water he claimed he could fish from his bedroom window. — Wikipedia
Julius Caesar conquered the Como area in 49 BC and resettled it with 5,000 colonists, founding "Novum Comum"; the Romans named the lake itself "Larius", the root of its modern name, Como. — Lake Como Tours
Villa d'Este in Cernobbio started life in 1568 as a cardinal's summer retreat, later passed through the hands of a ballerina, a Napoleonic general and an exiled queen, and only became a hotel in 1873. — Historic Hotels of the World
From parts of Cernobbio you genuinely can't tell where Italy ends and Switzerland begins – the town blends into Chiasso just across the invisible border on the forested slopes of Mount Bisbino. — Lake Como Travel
Harry's Bar in Cernobbio was opened in 1973 by Piero Sacchi, who wanted to bring the American cocktail-bar trend to Lake Como – its decor has barely changed since. — Harry's Bar Cernobbio

Wednesday 23rd September (Day 14) – Option B – Ferrari Maranello

The Ferrari Museum in Maranello opened on 18 February 1990 – deliberately chosen as the birthday of founder Enzo Ferrari, known as "the Drake", who had died two years earlier in 1988. — VisitModena
Enzo Ferrari personally test-drove every car his factory produced, but for his own daily journeys he had a soft spot for four-seaters – a preference that ran from the 1960 250 GT 2+2 to the 456 GT he approved in 1988. — Ferrari.com
The Ferrari Museum's futuristic entrance was designed by Renzo Piano, the same architect behind the Pompidou Centre in Paris – a design flourish for a factory that started out with a modest 1947 gate. — Ferrari.com
Next to the museum runs the 'Strada della Storia' (History Trail), a red pedestrian path through the park with plaques tracing a decade of Ferrari and Maranello history each. — Maranello Plus
Visitors to the museum can try a real Formula 1 pit-stop wheel change against the clock – the same task F1 crews do in under 2-3 seconds during a race. — Ferrari.com Museums
Maranello sits deep in Italy's balsamic vinegar country, and several local tour operators combine a Ferrari Museum visit with a traditional balsamic vinegar tasting tour – supercars and 12-year-aged vinegar, back to back. — Expedia

Wednesday 23rd September (Day 14) – Option C – Venice

The Republic of Venice was an independent maritime power for more than 1,100 years, from 697 AD until Napoleon deposed the last doge, Ludovico Manin, in 1797. — World History Encyclopedia
The enclosed Bridge of Sighs, built around 1600, connects the Doge's Palace interrogation rooms to the old prisons; its name comes from the sighs of condemned prisoners glimpsing their last view of Venice through its stone-barred windows. — Britannica
Venice's Acqua Alta bookshop keeps its stock safe from flooding canals by storing books inside full-size gondolas, bathtubs and even a rowing boat – when the water rises, the 'shelves' simply float. — Rosemary and Pork Belly
The city is built on more than 100 small islands, held up by wooden piles driven into the lagoon mud – starved of oxygen, the wood never rotted and instead petrified into something as hard as stone over the centuries. — Our Escape Clause
Tucked in Venice is the Scala Contarini del Bovolo, a spiralling external staircase so distinctive it gave the noble family who built it the nickname 'Bovolo' – Venetian dialect for 'snail'. — Atlas Obscura
Lazzaretto Nuovo, one of Venice's lagoon islands, was used as a plague quarantine station centuries ago and is linked to local legend of the so-called 'Vampire of Venice' – a skeleton found buried with a brick wedged in its jaw. — Atlas Obscura

Thursday 24th September (Day 15)

Regent's Canal, which runs past The Lighterman, was designed by architect John Nash – the same man behind Regent Street, Regent's Park and Buckingham Palace – and opened to great fanfare in 1820. — King's Cross
Granary Square, where The Lighterman sits, was once a Victorian canal basin where barges unloaded wheat for London's bakers; today the same spot features over 1,000 individually choreographed fountains. — King's Cross
In 1874 a barge loaded with gunpowder exploded under Macclesfield Bridge on Regent's Canal, killing four people, destroying the bridge and reportedly terrifying the animals at nearby London Zoo. — London Museum
The Coal Drops Yard arches near King's Cross weren't always shops and restaurants – in the Victorian era, gangs of famously tough, muscular women worked there unloading up to 30 wagon-loads of glass bottles a day for a bottle merchant. — King's Cross
Long before its boutique-shop makeover, the grimy Victorian coal-drop arches were home to the nightclub Bagley's, which packed in up to 2,500 clubbers on a Saturday night at the height of London's warehouse rave scene. — King's Cross

Friday 25th September (Day 16)

The Mousetrap began life as a short BBC radio play called 'Three Blind Mice', which Agatha Christie wrote as an 80th-birthday gift for Queen Mary in 1947, before she expanded it into the stage play in 1952. — Agatha Christie
The V&A's National Art Library holds more than 750,000 books, photographs and drawings, including works connected to Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks. — Victoria and Albert Museum
In March 1974 The Mousetrap moved from the Ambassadors Theatre to the St Martin's Theatre next door – and pulled off the entire transfer over a single weekend without missing one single performance. — Wikipedia
Agatha Christie was so sure The Mousetrap wouldn't last that she predicted it might run eight months. It has now passed 30,000 performances and is still the longest-running show of any kind in the world. — Wikipedia
The V&A's collection includes an antique French chair reputed to be haunted – visitors and staff have long claimed its cushion mysteriously deflates several times a day, as if someone invisible keeps sitting down. — Time Out London
Among the V&A's oddest objects is Tippoo's Tiger, a life-size 18th-century wooden automaton of a tiger mauling a British soldier – originally fitted with an organ mechanism that made the soldier's arm flail and produced groaning sounds. — Time Out London

Saturday 26th September (Day 17)

Hard Rock Cafe's now-famous memorabilia collection began right there in London in 1979, when regular customer Eric Clapton gave the cafe a signed Fender guitar; the venue today also houses 'The Vault', London's only rock-and-roll museum. — Hard Rock International
Six the Musical's writers modelled each of Henry VIII's wives on a real pop star – Catherine of Aragon channels Beyoncé, Anne Boleyn is Avril Lavigne/Lily Allen, Jane Seymour is Adele, Anne of Cleves is Nicki Minaj/Rihanna, and Katherine Howard is Ariana Grande/Britney Spears. — BBC Newsbeat
The Tower of London's ravens are technically enlisted members of the armed forces and can be formally 'dismissed' for misconduct – Raven George was sacked in 1986 for destroying television aerials and exiled to a zoo in Wales. — Wikipedia
Anne Boleyn's now-iconic space buns in Six the Musical weren't scripted – original West End cast member Millie O'Connell simply wore her hair that way at a 2018 preview, the creative team loved it, and it became the character's permanent look. — Beano

Sunday 27th September (Day 18)

Heathrow handled just 63,000 passengers in its first full year of operation in 1946; by 2025 that figure had grown to a record 84.5 million passengers in a single year. — Aerospace Global News
The Castle's current building on Cowcross Street, Farringdon, is Grade II listed and dates to 1865, sitting just off historic Smithfield Market in the City of London's square mile. — CAMRA
Despite terminals numbered 2 through 5, Heathrow has no Terminal 1 in use today – it opened in 1968 and was permanently closed in 2015 after 47 years of service. — Fact City
If Heathrow's control tower ever went out of action, a secret windowless backup replica of the tower's visual control room, hidden away from the airfield, can take over and keep up to 70% of flights running. — Surrey Live
Heathrow's Animal Reception Centre processes an extraordinary menagerie every year – around 28,000 fish, 2,000 birds and up to 200,000 reptiles pass through the airport. — Surrey Live
Nearby Farringdon has an oddly split identity: since 1394 it's been divided into 'Farringdon Within' and 'Farringdon Without', depending on which side of the old Roman London Wall each half fell on. — London x London
